title: AI Buildout Strains Spread From Equities Into Credit
content:
The window's defining shift was AI anxiety migrating from stock valuations into how the buildout is financed. The IMF named a possible AI-asset correction among its top stability risks, tallying roughly **$650bn** of related debt and a web of circular deals, while AI-linked bond issuance collapsed from over $100bn in June to about **$23bn** in September as banks including JPMorgan flagged tighter credit.

The stress showed up in prices. CoreWeave's bonds slid below **80 cents** on the dollar with spreads blowing out, chipmakers led a sell-off that dragged the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down over **4%** in a session, and the S&P 500, having printed a record above 7,800, ground to a weekly loss.

Crucially, the wobble handed Treasuries a renewed safe-haven bid, partly reversing the earlier rout. With much capex debt-funded, **circular financing** rather than AI demand became the market's swing factor, leaving hyperscaler leverage the key vulnerability into year-end.

title: Sticky Inflation Keeps a Fed Hike in Play and the Long End Elevated
content:
The higher-for-longer regime stayed the macro backbone. With the funds rate at **3.75%-4.00%** after September's hike, a hotter-than-expected September CPI revived bets on a further move at the late-October FOMC, and markets judged at least one more hike this year highly likely even as officials sent mixed signals.

Rates whipsawed. The 10-year, having earlier pressed above 5.3%, settled near **5.10%** and the 30-year around **5.44%**, while a firm dollar pushed towards multi-month highs. Late in the window yields eased as the AI-driven risk-off handed government debt a safe-haven bid.

The theme mattered because elevated discount rates pressured the richest equities, housing and credit, and kept the **term premium** story alive in the long end. Incoming inflation prints and the October decision remained the pivotal swing factors into year-end.

title: Middle East Supply Shock Lifts Crude to Multi-Month Highs
content:
A Middle East **supply shock** ran hard through the window. Attacks around the Strait of Hormuz cut transit flows to roughly two-thirds of their pre-war baseline, Houthi strikes hit Saudi energy infrastructure, and the collapse of a Russia-Ukraine energy truce stacked further supply risks.

Prices climbed accordingly. Brent settled near **$110**, its highest since May and up almost **5%** on the final week, while WTI jumped around **10%** to about **$101**, supported by a record US inventory draw.

The rally mattered beyond energy: higher crude fed directly into the hot inflation prints and hawkish rate rhetoric, reinforcing the higher-for-longer narrative. A durable recovery in Gulf flows would deflate the premium, but full normalisation likely hinges on a US-Iran understanding, leaving crude a key upside tail for inflation and a downside tail for risk.

title: Gold Consolidates Well Below Its Peak as Real Yields Bite
content:
Gold's pullback and consolidation became a cross-asset signal in its own right. After peaking near **$5,600** in January, bullion fell more than 8% in September and traded around **$4,150** through the window, pressured by multi-decade-high real yields and a firm dollar.

Yet the floor held. Central banks kept accumulating, with Q2 official purchases running near **290 tonnes**, and reserve diversification underpinned demand even as ETF investors trimmed holdings, a classic **debasement hedge** against large deficits and geopolitical risk.

The tension between policy headwinds and structural buying mattered: it left gold range-bound rather than trending, a barometer of whether safe-haven and diversification demand can offset the drag from elevated rates. Its behaviour into year-end remained a closely watched gauge of underlying investor anxiety.
